subtopic_detail: the order of volume replacement and bone directed therapy in a drowsy dehydrated woman whose creatinine has risen with the calcium
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 68 year old woman with breast cancer metastatic to bone who was brought in by her daughter. Over five days she has become increasingly drowsy, has vomited several times and has not opened her bowels.

Her daughter says she has been passing large volumes of urine and drinking very little, and that she slept most of yesterday. She takes no thiazide, no lithium and no calcium or vitamin D supplement, and she has had no recent imaging with contrast. Her creatinine three months ago was 78 micromol/L. She is rousable to voice and oriented to person only. Her mucous membranes are dry, her skin turgor is reduced and her jugular venous pressure is not visible with her lying flat.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not visible supine, chest clear, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.42 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45 to 90), urea 14.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), albumin 28 g/L (35 to 50), parathyroid hormone less than 0.5 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent given at a brisk rate with close monitoring
options.rationale: Hypercalcaemia drives a nephrogenic concentrating defect and vomiting, so these patients are always profoundly volume depleted, and restoring circulating volume alone lowers calcium by improving glomerular filtration and urinary calcium excretion. It must precede bone directed therapy because a bisphosphonate given to a hypovolaemic patient with an acute kidney injury risks worsening renal function. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)

options.text: Intravenous zoledronic acid at full dose given as a single infusion immediately
options.rationale: A bisphosphonate is the definitive treatment and will be given, but it takes two to four days to work, requires dose reduction in renal impairment and is relatively contraindicated until volume has been restored. Giving it first treats the number while leaving the physiology that caused it uncorrected. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide given regularly to promote a calcium diuresis from the outset
options.rationale: Loop diuretics were once routine but worsen volume depletion and electrolyte disturbance, and they are now reserved for fluid overload developing during rehydration in a patient with cardiac or renal impairment. Using one in a hypotensive hypovolaemic patient will make both the kidney injury and the calcium worse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral prednisolone at high dose with review of the calcium after forty eight hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are effective where the mechanism is excess calcitriol production, as in lymphoma, myeloma and granulomatous disease, but her suppressed parathyroid hormone with bone metastases indicates a parathyroid hormone related peptide or local osteolytic mechanism. The steroid is aimed at the wrong pathway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis against a low calcium bath arranged through the renal unit
options.rationale: Dialysis is reserved for life threatening hypercalcaemia with established kidney failure or heart failure that prevents adequate fluid loading, and her kidney injury is pre renal and expected to reverse with fluid. Escalating to dialysis before a saline challenge subjects her to an invasive procedure she is likely not to need. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy occurs in a substantial minority of patients with advanced cancer and carries a poor prognosis, marking disease progression as often as it marks a treatable metabolic emergency. Three mechanisms account for nearly all cases: secretion of parathyroid hormone related peptide by solid tumours, local osteolysis from bone metastases or myeloma, and excess calcitriol production in lymphoma and granulomatous disease, and the last of these is the one that responds to corticosteroid. A suppressed parathyroid hormone distinguishes these from primary hyperparathyroidism, which remains the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia overall and is usually mild and chronic rather than acute. The clinical syndrome of drowsiness, confusion, nausea, constipation, polyuria and polydipsia is explained by a calcium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that produces a vicious cycle of volume depletion and rising calcium. Management is therefore sequential: restore volume first, then give a bisphosphonate or denosumab to switch off osteoclastic resorption, then treat the underlying cancer.
key_points: Volume replacement comes before any bone directed agent
A suppressed parathyroid hormone separates malignant from primary hyperparathyroid hypercalcaemia
Bisphosphonates take two to four days to act and need renal dose adjustment
Corticosteroids work only in calcitriol mediated disease such as lymphoma or sarcoidosis
Loop diuretics are reserved for fluid overload during rehydration
explanation.pearls: Denosumab is the alternative when renal impairment precludes a bisphosphonate or when hypercalcaemia recurs despite one, because it is not renally cleared, but it carries a substantial risk of delayed hypocalcaemia and calcium must be monitored for several weeks afterwards.

subtopic_detail: a widespread rash with facial swelling, fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis appearing five weeks after starting a urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 62 year old man who was started on allopurinol by his general practitioner five weeks ago after a third attack of gout. He has had four days of feeling hot and shivery and a rash that began on his trunk and has spread.

He says his face feels tight and his wife says his eyelids and cheeks look puffy. The rash is itchy rather than painful. He has not taken any other new medication, has had no recent travel and no unwell contacts. On examination there is a confluent red rash covering most of his trunk and limbs with facial swelling, and there are enlarged tender nodes in both sides of his neck and in his axillae. His lips, mouth, eyes and genitals are normal with no erosions, and the skin does not shear when firm lateral pressure is applied.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform rash over more than half the body surface, periorbital and facial oedema, cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, no mucosal erosions, Nikolsky sign negative
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (less than 0.5), atypical lymphocytes present on film, alanine aminotransferase 320 U/L (less than 45), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60 to 110), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue allopurinol and add a sedating antihistamine with topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: Continuing the responsible drug in a reaction with fever, organ involvement and eosinophilia allows it to progress, and the mortality of this syndrome is around ten per cent, driven largely by liver failure. Antihistamine and topical treatment is the management of a simple morbilliform drug eruption, which this is not. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease allopurinol and commence systemic corticosteroid with staged organ monitoring
options.rationale: Withdrawal of the causative drug plus systemic corticosteroid is the standard treatment when there is significant organ involvement, and his transaminases at seven times the upper limit qualify. Monitoring continues for weeks after the drug is stopped because relapse and late thyroiditis are characteristic. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease allopurinol and arrange urgent transfer to the regional burns unit for care
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is the pathway for epidermal necrolysis, which presents with painful dusky skin, mucosal erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign, all of which are explicitly absent here. His rash is inflammatory rather than necrolytic and his skin barrier is intact. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease allopurinol and commence intravenous immunoglobulin over the next five days
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has been used in refractory cases and in epidermal necrolysis but has no established first line role in this syndrome, and it carries thrombotic and renal risks. It would be considered only after corticosteroid failure. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia)

options.text: Cease allopurinol and commence intravenous flucloxacillin for a presumed cellulitis
options.rationale: Cellulitis is unilateral, tender and sharply demarcated rather than a symmetrical confluent eruption with facial oedema, and it does not cause eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes or hepatitis. Adding a new beta lactam during a severe drug reaction also risks a second sensitisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction distinguished from ordinary drug exanthems by fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, haematological abnormality and internal organ involvement. Its defining feature is a long latency of two to eight weeks from starting the drug, far longer than the four to fourteen days of a simple morbilliform eruption, so the drug started most recently is frequently exonerated wrongly and an older one overlooked. Allopurinol, the aromatic anticonvulsants including carbamazepine, lamotrigine and phenytoin, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline account for most cases. The liver is the organ most often involved and hepatitis is the usual cause of death, while kidney, lung, heart and thyroid involvement also occur. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses is characteristic and contributes to the prolonged and relapsing course, which is why corticosteroid is weaned slowly over weeks to months and follow up thyroid function is checked months after apparent recovery.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks separates it from a simple drug exanthem
Fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy and eosinophilia are the recognition tetrad
Liver involvement is commonest and drives the mortality
Absent mucosal erosions and a negative Nikolsky sign exclude epidermal necrolysis
Relapse on steroid weaning and late autoimmune thyroid disease are characteristic
explanation.pearls: Check thyroid function two to three months after apparent recovery, because autoimmune thyroiditis develops weeks to months later in a recognised minority of patients and is easily missed once the rash has settled and the patient has been discharged.

subtopic_detail: multiple vertebral fractures fourteen months after the last six monthly injection in a woman who simply stopped attending
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71 year old woman who has had four days of severe pain between her shoulder blades that began as she lifted a box while unpacking after moving house.

She was treated with six monthly denosumab injections for five years for osteoporosis. She moved interstate fourteen months ago, did not transfer her care, and has had no injection since. She takes calcium and colecalciferol daily. She has had no fevers, no night sweats and no weight loss. Radiographs today show new wedge compression fractures at the seventh and ninth thoracic vertebrae that were not present on a film taken two years ago. Her serum and urine protein electrophoresis, corrected calcium, thyroid function and myeloma screen are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Tender over the mid thoracic spinous processes, increased thoracic kyphosis, normal lower limb neurology, height 4 cm less than recorded five years ago
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (greater than 50), thyroid stimulating hormone, creatinine and protein electrophoresis all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her osteoporosis now?

options.text: Continue calcium and colecalciferol alone and repeat bone densitometry in two years
options.rationale: Supplements support but do not substitute for antiresorptive therapy, and a woman who has already sustained two vertebral fractures has severe established disease with a high risk of further fractures within the next twelve months. Doing nothing active is the option with the highest short term fracture risk. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: Withhold all antiresorptive treatment until the acute fractures have healed fully
options.rationale: Fracture healing is not impaired by antiresorptive therapy and delaying treatment prolongs exactly the window of accelerated bone turnover that produced these fractures. The rebound is time limited but intense, so the delay is the harm. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: Recommence denosumab now and plan a bisphosphonate before it is ever stopped again
options.rationale: Stopping denosumab releases a burst of osteoclast activity that produces rapid bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures within one to two years, and the treatment is to restore antiresorptive suppression without further delay. The lasting fix is that denosumab is never simply ceased, and a bisphosphonate is given as follow on therapy whenever it is discontinued. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: Refer for percutaneous vertebroplasty of both fractured levels before any drug change
options.rationale: Vertebral augmentation has not shown consistent benefit over sham in randomised trials and is considered only for intractable pain unresponsive to conservative measures. It also addresses the two fractures already sustained rather than the accelerated bone loss that will cause the next ones. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Commence teriparatide alone as she has fractured while on antiresorptive treatment
options.rationale: Anabolic therapy has a place in severe osteoporosis with multiple fractures, but given immediately after denosumab and without antiresorptive cover it produces transient loss of hip bone density because it amplifies the already elevated turnover. The sequence of agents matters as much as the choice. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand, and unlike bisphosphonates it is not incorporated into bone, so its effect disappears entirely once dosing stops. The result is a rebound in osteoclast activity that overshoots baseline, producing rapid loss of the bone mineral density gained and a characteristic pattern of multiple vertebral fractures appearing within one to two years of the last injection. The risk is highest in those who had vertebral fractures before treatment and in those treated for longer, and a single late or missed dose is enough to begin the process. This makes denosumab a treatment that should not be started unless continuity can be assured, and it means a missed appointment carries a clinical consequence rather than an administrative one. When denosumab is deliberately stopped, a bisphosphonate is given as follow on therapy, usually starting around six months after the last injection, and bone turnover markers or densitometry are used to check that the rebound has been suppressed.
key_points: The denosumab effect ends completely when dosing stops, unlike a bisphosphonate
Rebound produces multiple vertebral fractures within one to two years
A single missed or delayed dose can initiate the rebound
Follow on bisphosphonate is mandatory whenever denosumab is ceased
Anabolic therapy given straight after denosumab without cover loses hip bone density
explanation.pearls: Denosumab injections are due every six months and are given within a four week window, so a patient who is more than a month overdue needs active recall rather than being left until the next routine visit.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

subtopic_detail: dusky coalescing macules with skin shearing and erosions at three mucosal sites three weeks after a rapidly titrated mood stabiliser
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who started lamotrigine three weeks ago for bipolar affective disorder and was titrated up quickly because of a transcription error on the prescription.

For two days she has had fever, a gritty burning sensation in both eyes and increasing pain in her mouth so that she cannot swallow her own saliva. Yesterday dusky flat spots appeared on her chest and have since joined together, and this morning the skin over her upper back and chest has begun to lift away in sheets. She describes the skin as burning and exquisitely painful rather than itchy. Gentle lateral pressure on apparently intact skin adjacent to a blister causes the epidermis to shear. Erosions are present on her lips, conjunctivae and vulva, and you estimate about twelve per cent of her body surface has detached.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, blood pressure 102/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dusky coalescing macules with flaccid blisters, epidermal detachment over about twelve per cent of body surface, positive Nikolsky sign, erosions of the lips, conjunctivae and vulva
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 4.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), urea 9.8 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22 to 32), glucose 6.8 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45 to 90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start oral prednisolone with review in clinic in two days
options.rationale: Ambulatory management is unsafe with twelve per cent epidermal detachment, since fluid loss, hypothermia, infection and ocular scarring all progress over the following days. The role of systemic corticosteroid in epidermal necrolysis also remains contested, unlike its accepted role in the eosinophilic drug syndrome. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and apply potent topical corticosteroid with oral antihistamine
options.rationale: Topical treatment is appropriate for inflammatory drug eruptions with an intact epidermis, whereas she has lost her skin barrier across a large area and needs the fluid, thermal, analgesic and ocular care of a specialist unit. Applying steroid to denuded dermis does not address any of those problems. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start intravenous flucloxacillin for staphylococcal skin disease
options.rationale: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is the near diagnosis to exclude, but it occurs almost entirely in young children, spares the mucosae and splits the epidermis at a very superficial level without the dusky targetoid macules seen here. Prophylactic antibiotics are also avoided in epidermal necrolysis because they select resistant organisms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and transfer urgently to a specialist burns or dermatology unit
options.rationale: Immediate withdrawal of the causative drug improves survival, and detachment of this extent requires the fluid balance, temperature control, analgesia, wound handling and ophthalmic review that only a specialist unit provides. Ocular involvement in particular causes permanent scarring and vision loss unless assessed within the first days. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Arrange a skin biopsy for frozen section before deciding on any transfer or treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy confirms the level of the split and is usually performed, but it is done alongside rather than before the decisions that determine survival. Waiting for histology delays drug withdrawal and transfer in a condition whose mortality tracks with how quickly the drug is stopped. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

explanation.summary: Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are a single disease separated by the extent of epidermal detachment, under ten per cent for the former, over thirty per cent for the latter, and the overlap band between them. Onset is typically one to four weeks after starting the responsible drug, with the aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, nevirapine and oxicam anti inflammatories the commonest culprits. A prodrome of fever, sore throat and painful eyes precedes the rash by one to three days and is routinely mistaken for a viral illness. Lamotrigine is a particular risk when titrated faster than the recommended schedule or combined with valproate, which inhibits its metabolism, so titration errors are a recurring cause. Mortality is predicted by the SCORTEN score using age, malignancy, heart rate, detached surface area, urea, bicarbonate and glucose, and early withdrawal of the causative drug is one of the few interventions with a clear survival benefit.
key_points: Detachment under ten per cent, ten to thirty per cent and over thirty per cent define the spectrum
Latency is one to four weeks and a febrile prodrome precedes the rash
Mucosal involvement at two or more sites with a positive Nikolsky sign is characteristic
Stopping the drug early is one of the few interventions that improves survival
Ophthalmology review within days prevents permanent ocular scarring
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly over at least six weeks, and the starting dose is halved when it is combined with valproate, because valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles its concentration.

subtopic_detail: recurrent severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen, hyponatraemia and new proximal weakness after a sulfonamide antibiotic
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to see a 27 year old woman in the emergency department with four days of severe generalised abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. She has been unable to keep anything down and has eaten almost nothing.

This is her third presentation with the same pain in eighteen months. A diagnostic laparoscopy eight months ago was entirely normal and she was told the pain was functional. Five days ago her general practitioner started trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. She has also been following a strict low carbohydrate diet for three weeks. Today she cannot lift her arms above her head to tie her hair and her grip has weakened. She is agitated and tearful and keeps asking to go home. Her partner mentions that the urine in the bottle by her bed went a deep reddish brown after sitting on the windowsill overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, blood pressure 156/94, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness but no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds present, proximal upper limb power 3 out of 5 with reduced biceps and supinator reflexes, sensation intact, no rash and no basophilic stippling reported on film
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 64 micromol/L (45 to 90), lipase and amylase within normal limits, haemoglobin 134 g/L (120 to 160), beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat computed tomography of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast
options.rationale: A normal contrast study three days into the illness, a soft abdomen without peritonism and a previously normal laparoscopy together make an intra abdominal structural cause very unlikely. Repeating the scan will not explain the hyponatraemia, the hypertension or the motor weakness. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Venous blood lead concentration with a blood film examined for basophilic stippling
options.rationale: Lead poisoning is the closest mimic, causing colicky abdominal pain with a motor neuropathy, but it produces a microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling and does not cause a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and her haemoglobin and film are normal. It is also not precipitated by starting a drug or by fasting. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

options.text: Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid protein and cell count to assess her weakness
options.rationale: An acute motor neuropathy makes Guillain Barre syndrome a reasonable thought, but that illness is ascending and predominantly distal, does not begin with four days of abdominal pain, and does not cause hypertension with hyponatraemia. Her weakness is proximal and upper limb predominant, which is the opposite of the usual pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Urine drug screen with paired serum and urine osmolality to explain the low sodium
options.rationale: Paired osmolalities would confirm inappropriate antidiuresis but stop at describing a mechanism that is itself a manifestation of the underlying disease rather than an answer. Investigating the sodium in isolation leaves the pain, the hypertension and the weakness unexplained. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Urinary porphobilinogen measured on a fresh sample protected from light exposure
options.rationale: Recurrent severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging, autonomic features of tachycardia and hypertension, a motor neuropathy, hyponatraemia and psychiatric disturbance, all following a sulfonamide and a period of carbohydrate restriction, is the acute neurovisceral attack of a hepatic porphyria. Porphobilinogen rises markedly during an attack and the sample is shielded from light because the porphyrins degrade on exposure. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

explanation.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria is the commonest of the acute hepatic porphyrias and results from partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase, so that induction of hepatic haem synthesis floods the pathway with neurotoxic porphyrin precursors. Attacks are provoked by anything that induces the rate limiting enzyme, principally drugs including sulfonamides, barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin and progestogens, along with fasting or carbohydrate restriction, alcohol, infection and the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. The attack is neurovisceral rather than cutaneous: severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and no peritonism, autonomic overactivity with tachycardia and hypertension, a predominantly motor and often proximal neuropathy that can ascend to respiratory failure, hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuresis, and psychiatric disturbance ranging from anxiety to frank psychosis. Patients are characteristically investigated repeatedly and frequently undergo a negative laparotomy or laparoscopy before the diagnosis is considered, so a history of recurrent unexplained abdominal pain with normal imaging is itself a diagnostic clue. Treatment is withdrawal of the precipitant, high carbohydrate intake, and intravenous haem arginate, with careful attention to using only drugs known to be safe in porphyria.
key_points: Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen and normal imaging is the hallmark
Autonomic features, motor neuropathy, hyponatraemia and psychiatric change complete the syndrome
Sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, rifampicin, progestogens, fasting and alcohol precipitate attacks
Urinary porphobilinogen during the attack is the diagnostic test and the sample must be light protected
Treatment is removal of the precipitant, carbohydrate loading and intravenous haem arginate
explanation.pearls: Every drug prescribed during and after an attack must be checked against a porphyria safe list, and among the analgesics morphine and paracetamol are safe while among the antiemetics ondansetron is safe but metoclopramide is a recognised precipitant.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists
